Autopilot: You instinctively search for consensus—choosing what the group would approve of, what fits your social role, or what keeps your most valuable relationships intact. Your personal opinion is sidelined so thoroughly that you lose track of what you actually want. Awareness: What would the group decide, and what would you decide? Are you still able to tell the difference right now? Exercise: Make this decision entirely on your own in silence first. Write down your choice before you talk it over with anyone else. Then compare the two.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SO2. Autopilot: You try to bridge the crisis by offering advice, support, and caretaking—for everyone else involved. Your own hurt remains unexpressed. You know exactly what the other person needs to fix things, but you have no idea what you need. Awareness: Are you trying to solve this relationship crisis by playing the helper, or by genuinely showing up? What would happen if you stopped managing the situation and just sat with it? Exercise: Pause in the middle of this crisis and ask the other person, "How are you really doing?" Then just listen—no advice, no fixes, no offers to help. Just hold the space.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SO2. Autopilot: You doubt whether you are truly important to people, rather than just useful. When no one checks in on you, it confirms your deepest internal fear: Without my contribution, I am invisible. Awareness: Who actually knows you—not what you do, but who you are? And have you genuinely allowed anyone to see the real you lately? Exercise: Call someone today and say, "I just need to talk—not to fix anything, but because I need to be heard." Observe how it feels to step out of the strong role.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SO2. Autopilot: You carry the grief of the community, completely forgetting your own. The group gives you a sense of belonging and structure, but you remain out on the perimeter: always available, rarely visible in your own pain. Awareness: Whose pain are you actually carrying right now—yours or the collective's? Is there a safe space where your own loss is allowed to show its face? Exercise: Find a moment of absolute quiet today, exclusively for you and your loss. No processing conversations, no tasks. Just you and what you have genuinely lost.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SO2. Autopilot: You are there for everyone else, completely bypassing yourself. The group needs your backing, so you give it—even when your own tank is completely empty. Recharging your own battery gets pushed off because it feels selfish. Awareness: What do you need right now—truly you, not the community? And have you given yourself permission to have it today? Exercise: Carve out one hour today entirely for yourself—no tasks, no people, no obligations. Do something that genuinely fills you up. Notice if you feel guilty allowing yourself to take it.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SO2. Autopilot: Without a community to serve or validation to receive, life feels flat and hollow. You instantly go hunting for new projects, new people, or new groups to join—using activity to fill the void rather than facing it. Awareness: What is left of you when no group needs you? Is there something inside you that holds inherent value, even without an audience? Exercise: Spend an evening entirely by yourself tonight—no social media, no plans. Watch what bubbles up to the surface in the quiet. What is it that you truly need?

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: Your exhaustion stems from pouring intense energy into a connection—and when that relationship doesn't give back what you hoped for, you double down and invest even more. Your intensity spikes even as your energy drains away. Awareness: What would happen if you didn't give anything of yourself right now—if you simply received? Can you let that happen without immediately feeling the urge to match or return it? Exercise: Today, allow someone to give you something—a gesture, a kind word, an offer of help. Accept it without offering anything in return. Sit for a moment with the raw sensation of pure receiving.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: In a conflict, you crank up the emotional intensity. The underlying question driving you is always: Do you really love me? Do you even see me? Your accusations can be incredibly passionate and direct—often completely overwhelming the other person. Awareness: What are you actually trying to say beneath all that intensity? Would it be possible to just state it directly and simply—without the dramatic framework? Exercise: Try speaking what you desire in a completely calm, grounded tone, focusing strictly on your needs rather than what the other person did wrong. Observe whether this quiet approach shifts the dynamic.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: Loneliness is experienced as a painful lack of total fusion—as if the connection isn't intense enough or the other person isn't truly present. Your immediate instinct is to get even more intense, go deeper, and demand more. Awareness: Is this loneliness a sign that the connection is missing, or is it a signal that you are currently disconnected from yourself? Exercise: Sit by yourself for a while today—deliberately, as a conscious choice. Ask yourself: Who am I when no one else is mirroring me? What is left of me when the connection takes a temporary pause?

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: You anchor your decision entirely around the most important person in your life: What would they choose? What will bring us closer together? Your own voice goes completely quiet under the massive weight of the relationship. Awareness: Which part of this decision are you making for yourself, and which part are you making solely for the sake of the relationship? Are you absolutely sure the other person even wants you to sacrifice your preference? Exercise: Make this decision completely on your own first—then simply state it to the other person. Share it as a neutral piece of information, not as a question. Notice how it feels to claim that space.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: The intensity escalates: you demand more radical honesty, more closeness, more real intimacy. If the other person can't or won't meet you there, you plunge into a deep, icy, punishing withdrawal. Beneath it all lies the core terror: Am I truly loved? Awareness: What if the other person is currently giving you the absolute best they can—and their limitation isn't a sign of indifference, but just a personal boundary? Can you look at it from that perspective? Exercise: Ask your partner directly: "What are you realistically able to give me in this crisis right now?" Focus on what they are capable of, not what you want. Listen to their answer without analyzing or judging it.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: Your self-doubt zeroes in on one core question: Am I truly desirable to this person? If they don't respond, don't ask about you, or don't show affection, you conclude that something is fundamentally wrong with you. Your inner critic turns self-destructive. Awareness: Is the other person's withdrawal actually a reflection of your worth, or is it just a reflection of their own internal state? Can you separate the two? Exercise: Write down what makes you inherently lovable—not what you bring to the relationship or give to the other person, but who you are for yourself. Read it over when the doubt starts getting loud.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: Loss cuts you to the very core, especially when it involves a central relationship. You try to convert the pain into raw devotion: you chase closeness and surrender yourself completely—or you flip to the exact opposite extreme, locking down as protection against further hurt. Awareness: What do you actually need right now—closeness or space? And can you clearly state what you need without playing a game? Exercise: Today, write a letter to the person or thing you have lost. Say everything you never got the chance to say. There is no audience, no expectations—just your raw truth.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: Overwhelm is triggered by the sheer intensity of your giving within your primary relationship. You give everything, expect everything, and when the equilibrium tips, you exhaust yourself by completely capitulating or aggressively pulling away. Awareness: What are you trying to give right now that you don't even have in your own emotional tank? What would it look like to draw a firm line here? Exercise: Today, tell the most important person in your life exactly what you need right now—not what you can do for them. Just say: "Right now, I need..." and give them the space to respond.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SX2. Autopilot: Without an intense connection to focus on, life feels completely flat, hollow, and meaningless. You immediately go hunting for the next spark, the next deep encounter—using intensity as an antidote to the emptiness. Awareness: What if the emptiness is actually just a quiet breathing room, rather than a sign that something is wrong? Can you let the stillness just be still? Exercise: Sit quietly with yourself today. Twenty minutes, entirely disconnected from the outside world. Ask yourself: What is it that I truly want—outside of my next relationship?

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: Reaching for the next task happens automatically. Exhaustion is treated as an efficiency problem rather than a need for rest. Your solution: organize better, move faster, restructure the to-do list. Awareness: What happens to you—the human being behind the tasks—when the work pauses? Who are you when you aren't producing anything? Exercise: Sit for a few minutes without a screen and without a task. Observe how quickly your mind drifts to the next thing that needs to get done—and notice what lies underneath when it doesn't.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: In a conflict, your instinct is to resolve it quickly or simply move past it. Emotions put the brakes on efficiency, so they get pushed aside. You just want the conflict to end so everyone can get back to making progress. Awareness: What is being bypassed right now just because it would slow down the solution? And wouldn't it actually be more efficient to address the real root of the issue? Exercise: Allow yourself to stay in a conflict a moment longer than you normally would. Ask yourself: What hasn't been said yet that actually matters?

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: Loneliness is barely registered because you stay so busy. If it does surface, your response is to add more appointments, more projects, and more contacts. Connection is treated like an optimization problem—something to manage rather than to feel. Awareness: When was the last time you felt a genuine sense of contact—not networking, not coordination, but real connection? How long has it been? Exercise: Make plans to hang out with someone—with absolutely no agenda. No goal, no expected outcome. Just time together. Observe how that feels.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: You pick the option that looks best and gets you to the goal the fastest. Decisions are made to keep things moving forward, not to prompt reflection. Doubts are skipped over because they slow down your momentum. Awareness: Are you making this decision because it's truly right, or simply because you want to get moving again? Is there something you're missing because you refuse to pause? Exercise: Put the decision on hold for 24 hours. The next morning, ask yourself again: Is this still the right choice? If it is, then take action.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: A crisis is treated as a problem that needs to be solved efficiently. You analyze, propose solutions, and try to move past it. The actual emotional dimension—what the other person is truly feeling, and what you are feeling—gets skipped entirely. Awareness: What are you trying to fix right now—the problem, or the relationship? And does the other person know that you are genuinely present, not just functioning? Exercise: Set the solutions aside for a moment. Simply ask: "How are you really doing?" And then, wait until the real answer emerges.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: Self-doubt disguises itself as a performance issue: I didn't do well enough, I wasn't efficient enough, I presented myself poorly. The deeper question—Am I enough?—remains buried under the workload. Awareness: What if you didn't achieve anything right now—what would be left of you? And would that person be enough? Exercise: Sit today for five minutes with no task. When the self-doubt creeps in, label it: "That is performance anxiety." Then ask: Who am I if it's right—and who am I if it's wrong?

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: Loss is bridged by sheer activity: the next project, the next task, the next goal. Pain is viewed as an obstacle to productivity. Eventually, it breaks through in an entirely unexpected place. Awareness: What if you didn't accomplish anything today, and just grieved? What would that say about you, and is that story actually true? Exercise: Set aside an hour today with no tasks. If the pain comes up, let it. If it doesn't, just sit in the stillness anyway. Both are allowed.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: Being overwhelmed is either ignored or used as fuel: more efficiency, better systems, faster processes. You optimize your way through the pressure instead of stopping. Eventually, your body goes on strike. Awareness: What if pausing today was actually the most productive thing you could possibly do? What is pushing through really costing you? Exercise: Take a deliberate break today—no working, no optimizing, no planning. Just twenty minutes. Sit there, and observe how long it takes before you start feeling restless.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SE3. Autopilot: Without tasks and successes, you face an identity crisis: Who am I if I'm not achieving anything right now? Stagnation is aggressively fought off with new projects instead of being endured. Awareness: Who are you when you aren't hitting milestones? Is there a part of you that exists completely independent of your performance? Exercise: Today, write down the answer to this question: Who am I without my achievements, without my successes, and without my goals? Let the answer come, even if it feels empty at first.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: The image must be maintained at all costs—even when you are completely out of energy. To the outside world, everything is running smoothly. Exhaustion is never shown because it would damage the presentation. You keep performing until you hit an absolute wall. Awareness: What version of yourself are you working so hard to project right now, and for whose benefit? Who would still truly see you if that curtain dropped for just a moment? Exercise: Radically admit to yourself how you are actually doing. No spin, no audience. Just you and your actual, raw state—name it for what it is, without trying to fix it right away.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: In a conflict, the spotlight quickly shifts to the question: How do I look right now? Defending your image can easily become more important than actually resolving the root issue. Awareness: Are you defending yourself right now, or are you defending your reputation? What would shift if you could clearly see the difference between the two? Exercise: In the middle of a conflict, ask yourself: What would I say right now if there were absolutely no onlookers? Speak directly from that place.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: Loneliness is incredibly difficult to tolerate because it feels like you vanish when there's no audience. Your immediate instinct is to become more visible, achieve more, and polish your image—believing that as long as others see you, you exist. Awareness: Do you still exist when the spotlight is turned off? What is left of you when absolutely no one is watching? Exercise: Spend some time with yourself today—no mirrors, no performance. Write down who you are when you don't have an audience. Don't list your achievements; focus strictly on you.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: You make decisions based on external optics: What looks good? What enhances my status? The internal question isn't What is right? but rather What plays well?—which often pulls your choices in a direction that doesn't feel true to you. Awareness: What would you choose if no one ever found out—no status points, no external validation, no applause? Do you even know what that answer is? Exercise: Write down the decision that you know deep down is right for you, even if it looks entirely unimpressive on paper. Then, ask yourself if you have the courage to choose it anyway.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: The crisis is kept completely invisible to the outside world—the optics of the relationship must look perfect. Internally, you work tirelessly on a solution that saves face. What the other person actually feels takes a back seat to the question: How do we look to others? Awareness: Are you currently holding up the weight of this relationship, or are you just holding up the illusion of it? Do you actually know what your partner needs right now? Exercise: Have a conversation today that aims to solve nothing and optimize nothing. Simply ask: "How are we actually doing?" Resist the urge to fix it. Just listen.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: Your self-doubt revolves entirely around your image: Am I being well-received? Do they see me the way I want them to? Your inner critic constantly compares your public profile with everyone else's and always finds a gap. Awareness: What if you dropped the defensive exterior right now and just allowed yourself to be present? Would anyone who truly loves you value you any less? Exercise: Tell someone you trust completely exactly how you're doing today—no filters, no positive spin. Just the unvarnished truth. Notice what that shifts inside you.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: You stay strong, even in the midst of grief; the appearance of high-level functioning must be maintained. Internally, the pain runs deep, but it isn't allowed center stage because it disrupts the narrative of your competence. Awareness: What would the people who matter most to you say if you showed weakness today? Would the world actually fall apart if you did? Exercise: Confide in someone you trust about how you are truly holding up right now—without trying to protect your image. Just give them the raw truth about your pain.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: You project absolute competence and total control to the outside world, even when everything inside feels like it's collapsing. The facade of functioning stays up right until a breakdown becomes inevitable. Awareness: What would happen if you admitted to someone today that it's just too much? Would it really destroy your image, or would it just make you human? Exercise: Tell someone you trust explicitly: "It's just too much right now." Stop there. No plan, no immediate solution. Just observe what changes after you say it.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SO3. Autopilot: Stagnation feels like a direct threat to your image: you no longer look dynamic, forward-moving, or successful. You exhaust yourself trying to camouflage the standstill from the outside world. Awareness: What would happen if you admitted to someone today that you're currently feeling stuck? Would that truly shatter the picture they have of you? Exercise: Confess to someone you trust today: "I honestly don't know where I'm headed right now." Leave out the plan or the fix. Observe what happens next.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: You mask your exhaustion with intensity and charisma—especially around the person who matters most to you. You project an image of strength and indispensability. Letting your guard down feels like losing. Awareness: What would the person closest to you see if you stopped pretending right now? And would that really be so terrible? Exercise: Honestly share with someone close to you just how exhausted you are—not disguised as a weakness, but simply stated as a fact. Observe what that shifts inside you and within the connection.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: In a conflict, an impulse to win takes over. It stops being just about the issue at hand and becomes about maintaining the upper hand. Arguments are weaponized as tools to convince or outmaneuver the other person. Awareness: Do you want to be right in this moment, or do you want to be understood? Those are two very different things. Exercise: For once in this conflict, validate the other person's strongest point. Say out loud, "You're right about that." Observe what that stirs up inside you.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: Loneliness validates a deep-seated inner narrative: Ultimately, I am not desirable. Your instinct is to become even more charismatic, more attractive, and more fascinating—believing that as long as the other person desires you, you aren't truly alone. Awareness: What if someone could love you in this exact moment—just as you are, without the facade? Could you actually let yourself believe that? Exercise: Today, write down what you appreciate about yourself—not what you can do, and not what you achieve. What is inherently lovable about you, even when you are completely alone?

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: You cater your decisions to the person who matters most to you: What will impress them? What makes me look more attractive, valuable, or indispensable in their eyes? Your own voice is barely even audible. Awareness: Are you making this choice for yourself, or for the image you want to create in their mind? What would you choose if absolutely no one were scoring it? Exercise: Write down what you would choose if this person were never going to find out about your decision. That answer is much closer to your true self.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: The crisis becomes a trial: Are they truly committed to me? Does this connection hold up when things get heavy? You demand closeness, clarity, and reassurance—and if the other person doesn't deliver, you either freeze them out or escalate. Awareness: What if the other person is simply overwhelmed by this crisis right now—and it isn't actually a sign that they don't love you? Exercise: Today, ask your partner a specific question: "What do you need from me right now—in a single sentence?" Then just listen, without evaluating their answer.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: Your self-doubt targets your attractiveness and impact on the person who matters most: Am I truly captivating enough for them? Is my spark fading? Your inner critic constantly compares you to others and always finds a flaw. Awareness: What if the other person doesn't love you for the effect you have on them, but simply for who you are? Can you open yourself up to believing that right now? Exercise: Ask your partner today: "What do you value about me—not what I do, but who I am?" Listen to the answer without immediately deflecting or downplaying it.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: Loss—especially a loss of status or the breakdown of a relationship—hits you deeply. You react by either withdrawing entirely or doubling down on your efforts: trying to be even better, more attractive, and more irreplaceable. Awareness: What if you didn't have to try harder or be better in the face of this loss, but were simply allowed to grieve? What remains when you stop trying to shine? Exercise: Today, write down what this loss actually means to you—not what it means for your image, but what it means to you deeply as a human being.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: When overwhelmed, you channel that pressure into performing for your primary person: you want to impress them, be irreplaceable, and shine—even when you are internally at your absolute limit. Awareness: What if the other person cherishes you even when you aren't putting on a stellar performance? Are you allowed to just be? Exercise: Tell the person who matters most to you honestly how you are doing today—no polish, no performance. Simply say, "I'm just really overwhelmed right now." Then see how they respond.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SX3. Autopilot: Stagnation feels like the death of your magnetic pull: it feels like you've lost your luster, your energy, and your impact. You immediately start to withdraw or go hunting for a new spark. Awareness: What if the other person values you just as much during this quiet phase—without the high energy and achievements? Can you allow that to be true? Exercise: Spend time with the person who matters most to you today without any staging or performing. Just be in the room together. Observe what naturally unfolds between you.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Exhaustion is endured in silence. You don't complain, you show very little—but you suffer. Your internal withdrawal deepens, and at some level, the exhaustion confirms an old narrative: life is heavy, and this is just the burden you carry. Awareness: Are you carrying this exhaustion alone because you believe no one would truly understand it? What if someone could carry it—right alongside you? Exercise: Write down everything you are carrying right now—no sugarcoating, no downplaying. Then read it out loud, as if you were telling it to a trusted friend. Observe how that shifts things.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: In a conflict, you retreat inward. You carry the hurt, sometimes for a very long time, without the other person ever knowing how deeply it cuts. Very little on the outside—a universe on the inside. Awareness: What are you currently holding inside that the other person has no idea about—and what would happen if you actually said it? Exercise: Name what hurt you, just this once—calmly, clearly, without any drama. Simply say: "That hurt me because..." Leave the sentence open-ended if you need to.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Loneliness is quietly endured—and, at the same time, deepened. You turn inward, nurturing the melancholy, writing, dreaming, feeling. The solitude takes on a dark beauty, which makes reaching out to the outside world even harder. Awareness: Is your withdrawal protecting you right now, or is it keeping you trapped where you suffer? What would a single, tiny step outward look like? Exercise: Write a note to someone you miss—and actually send it. It doesn't need to be long. Just: I'm thinking of you.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Every option becomes loaded with internal meaning: What does this choice say about who I am? What will be lost forever if I choose differently? A simple decision becomes an existential crisis rather than a practical choice. Awareness: How much weight are you forcing onto this decision? And is it truly that final—or does it just feel that way? Exercise: Write down what you would lose with each option. Then write down what you would gain. Let both lists sit side-by-side, giving them equal value.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: You carry the crisis silently—swallowing an immense amount internally while showing very little on the outside. You hold onto the hurt, sometimes for weeks. When it finally surfaces, it comes out deep, heavy, and intense. Awareness: Are you carrying this crisis alone because you believe the other person can't truly understand it—or have you actually given them a real chance to try? Exercise: In a quiet moment today, tell your partner what is truly weighing on you in the relationship—not an accusation, but the actual core pain. Just one sentence.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Your self-doubt is existential: I am fundamentally different, and different means defective. The inner narrative deepens: Others have it easier; life is just more accessible to them. I am either too much or not enough—never just right. Awareness: What if "being different" isn't a statement about a deficit—but simply a description? Who decided that different automatically means wrong? Exercise: Write down three things about your way of being that are valuable—not despite your depth, but precisely because of it. Read them out loud and let them carry weight for a moment.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Loss is felt deeply and often carried entirely alone. The pain becomes the very core of your identity: I am the one who loses, the one who is lacking. The grief hardens into place instead of moving through you. Awareness: What if this loss doesn't define you, but simply touches you? And is there a part of you beyond the pain that belongs to you, too? Exercise: Today, write down: What did I learn or experience through this loss that I didn't know before? Not to romanticize the pain—but to see the whole picture.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Being overwhelmed is felt intensely and usually carried alone. The pressure mixes with self-blame: Why can't I handle this? Others seem to carry this so much more effortlessly. Your isolation grows. Awareness: What if the way you feel this pressure doesn't mean you are weaker—but simply that you feel things more deeply? What would actually comfort you right now? Exercise: Today, write down exactly what is too much—honestly, without any self-criticism. Then read it out loud like a matter-of-fact report: This is what is. No more, no less.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SE4. Autopilot: Stagnation and internal emptiness feel familiar—and dangerously comfortable. You sink into them, making them your home. The longing for intensity remains, but you lack the energy to go looking for it. Awareness: What if this emptiness isn't the end—but rather a blank canvas where something new can begin? What might be quietly trying to take root right now? Exercise: Create something small today—a sentence, a sketch, a single line. Not for anyone else. Just to put something out there against the silence. That is enough.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: Your exhaustion becomes visible—and at the same time, it is accompanied by deep shame. You constantly compare yourself to others who seemingly navigate life with much more ease. The exhaustion only confirms your internal narrative that you are somehow falling behind. Awareness: What if your exhaustion isn't a badge of inadequacy, but rather proof that you live life with true emotional intensity? Would something shift inside you if you looked at it that way? Exercise: Today, write down a single sentence about your exhaustion—not as a complaint, but as a neutral observation. "I am exhausted"—and then take a breath. Nothing more.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: In a conflict, your sense of hurt becomes massive and highly visible. You feel deeply misunderstood, dismissed, or unseen—which immediately validates an old internal wound. Comparison creeps in: Other people never seem to struggle with this the way I do. Awareness: Are you actually arguing about this specific conflict right now—or are you reacting to an older pain that this moment has accidentally triggered? Exercise: Separate what is happening today from what belongs to the past. Describe exactly what happened in this conversation in one objective sentence. Only then ask yourself: What old wound did it touch?

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: Loneliness fuels the habit of comparison: Others have real connections; others know how to belong. You pull back into the role of the outsider, watching from the fringes as everyone else's lives unfold—and feeling the painful ache of the distance. Awareness: What exactly do you see in others that you secretly wish for yourself? And how much of that is truly out of your reach, and how much is just untried? Exercise: Do one small thing today that makes connection possible—even if it feels awkward or unpolished. Send a quick text, start a casual conversation. Don't worry about it being perfect. Just make it real.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: You obsess over what choices others are making—and constantly measure yourself against them. What does someone like me choose? What do the people who actually belong choose? Your own true voice is barely audible because your mind is always in comparison mode. Awareness: What is it that you actually want—completely free of comparisons, benchmarks, or reference points? Is there a quiet intuition inside you that you keep drowning out? Exercise: Ask yourself: What would I choose right now if I had absolutely no idea what anyone else would choose in this situation? Write that answer down and anchor yourself to it.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: You fall into the comparison trap—comparing your partnership to other couples, other dynamics, or an idealized fantasy. In a crisis, this relationship feels like definitive proof: Others have it easier; something is fundamentally wrong with me. Awareness: What if this relationship is simply exactly how relationships can be sometimes—messy, unfinished, and yet completely real? What would you do from this vantage point? Exercise: Write down what this relationship has genuinely given you—focusing on concrete examples, not abstract ideals. Take that list with you into the conversation that needs to happen.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: You compare yourself to others—and you always end up losing. Everyone else seems more secure, more grounded, more normal. Your self-doubt whispers a familiar story: I am missing a vital piece that everyone else has. Awareness: What if this comparison is completely unfair because you are comparing your messy internal reality to everyone else's polished external facade? What do you actually know about their inner lives? Exercise: Today, write down what specifically sets you apart from others, and focus on why that difference is valuable. Don't focus on the perceived lack. Focus on your unique contribution.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: You feel loss deeply—and immediately begin to compare: Others lose things too, but for me it's different, heavier, lonelier. Your pain takes on a unique coloring that simultaneously connects you to humanity and isolates you from it. Awareness: What if your pain is neither smaller nor greater than anyone else's—but simply yours to hold? How would it feel to carry it without constantly measuring it? Exercise: Connect with someone today who has also experienced loss—without turning it into a comparison. Just listen to one another. Let their pain sit comfortably alongside yours, rather than competing with it.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: You measure yourself against the room: Others seem to handle this exact same pressure so much better. The self-doubt underlying your overwhelm makes the burden twice as heavy. You withdraw into isolation instead of asking for help. Awareness: What if you reached out for support today—not because you are weak, but because you are a human being with real, valid boundaries? Exercise: Ask one specific person for a tangible piece of help today. Don't just say a general "I'm overwhelmed," but offer a clear request: "Could you take over this specific task for me?"

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SO4. Autopilot: Stagnation triggers the comparison loop: Others are moving, growing, and experiencing life. I am completely stuck. The pain of this realization hardens into a core conviction: I am fundamentally flawed. Awareness: What if the people you are watching are secretly feeling stuck too, and you just can't see it? What alive qualities are still resting inside you right now? Exercise: Today, write down three things that are vibrantly alive within you—not what you do, but who you are. A personality trait, a core value, or an inherent gift. Let them be enough.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: When exhaustion sets in, your internal demands only escalate—both for yourself and for others. You weaponize emotional intensity as an antidote to inner emptiness. You demand more, expect more, and give more, until you hit an absolute wall. Awareness: What is actually driving all this intensity right now? Is it true passion, or is it a deep-seated fear of what you might discover if everything suddenly became quiet? Exercise: Pause in the middle of a highly intense moment and ask yourself: What am I actually feeling beneath all this electricity? Take a single deep breath. Simply name whatever surfaces, without trying to instantly transform it.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: In a conflict, you demand more depth, more radical honesty, and more intensity. You reject superficial quick fixes out of hand. You need the other person to truly see what is at stake—which can end up creating immense pressure. Awareness: Is the level of emotional intensity you are demanding realistically achievable for the other person right now, or are you cranking it up so high that it actually drives them away? Exercise: Try stating what you truly need in plain, simple terms—free of any dramatic framing. Focus not on what the other person should be doing, but solely on what you need.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: Loneliness cuts you incredibly deep because your longing for absolute fusion is so powerful. At the same time, you preemptively guard against it: you believe that if no one gets close, no one can hurt you. Your withdrawal serves as both a shield and a prison. Awareness: Are you keeping your distance because you genuinely need peace, or because closeness terrifies you? What if both of those things could be true at the exact same time? Exercise: Give yourself permission to reveal a small piece of true vulnerability to someone today. Not the whole universe—just one authentic moment. Observe what that shifts within the connection.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: Every choice turns into an internal battle: Which option is genuinely authentic? Which one is truly me? No path feels entirely whole; each one feels somehow lacking. The decision loops endlessly in the orbit of an impossible ideal. Awareness: Is there an option on the table that simply feels the most alive—even if it isn't perfect? What if that were allowed to be enough? Exercise: Choose the option that resonates most clearly in your body, rather than the one your intellect tries to validate as correct. Then stand by it, unpolished as it may be.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: A crisis triggers intense, immediate demands from you: more authenticity, more depth, more raw honesty—right now. When the other person can't keep pace, it confirms your oldest suspicion: No one is capable of truly holding the weight of what I need. Awareness: Is what you are demanding right now actually what the crisis requires to heal—or is it what you have always longed for and never managed to receive? Exercise: Tell your partner exactly one thing you want from them right now—something concrete, achievable, and possible today. Not the entire relationship overhaul, just this single step.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: Your self-doubt becomes heavy, intense, and dark: Am I actually being authentic? Have I lost myself? Was what I just showed real, or was it just a performance? Your inner critic relentlessly dissects your deep layers, looking for any trace of falsehood. Awareness: What if the very fact that you are doubting is proof of your authenticity? After all, only someone who feels deeply could ever doubt themselves this thoroughly. Could that be true too? Exercise: Write down exactly what you are feeling in this exact moment—without shaping it, without dressing it up. Just raw text. That is you. That is real.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: You experience loss with overwhelming intensity. The pain can completely flood your world, channeled into art, deep isolation, or heavy conversations. Sometimes, suffering itself becomes a badge of connection: The more deeply I hurt, the more authentically I live. Awareness: What if your pain remains entirely real even as it begins to quiet down? Does grief always have to be deafening to be true? Exercise: Channel something out of your loss today—a drawing, a written line, a collage. Not to show it off to an audience. Simply to give the pain a physical form that can help carry it.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: Being overwhelmed breaks through in dramatic waves: either as a sudden creative obsession, a raw emotional outburst, or a total, freezing withdrawal. Your mood swings violently—from burning bright to completely burnt out. Awareness: What is it that you truly need in this exact moment—to pull back into isolation, or to reach out for connection? And do you know who can realistically offer that to you? Exercise: Give the pressure a tangible outlet today: write it out, sketch it, or move your body. Don't try to solve the underlying problem—just discharge the raw energy so you can see clearly again.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SX4. Autopilot: Without emotional intensity, life feels flat and dead. You instinctively reach for the next heavy experience, the next deep encounter, the next wave of pain or rush of excitement—anything to avoid sitting face-to-face with the void. Awareness: What if the quiet stillness is actually the most intense experience available to you—if you were brave enough to truly meet it? Exercise: Sit quietly with the emptiness today for twenty minutes—without trying to fill it, without trying to escape it. Afterward, write down a single sentence: What did I actually hear in the silence?

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: Stagnation triggers even more withdrawal: you read, ponder, and hoard information—but you don't take action. Analyzing the stagnation ends up replacing the act of breaking through it. The retreat morphs into a comfortable habit. Awareness: What is the smallest possible step you could take toward the outside world right now—not the perfect step, just the smallest one? What if you took it today? Exercise: Choose one specific thing that you have known how to do for a long time but haven't actually executed. Do it within the next twenty minutes. Do not prepare—just start.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: In conflict comes withdrawal. You need distance, time, silence - to process what happened. On the outside it seems cold or disinterested, even though there is a lot going on inside. Awareness: Does the other person need a signal from you that you are still there - even if you need time to process it? Exercise: Briefly tell the other person what you need: "I need some time to process this. I'll be back." This closes the connection instead of cutting it off.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: Loneliness is almost a normal state for the SE5 - familiar, controlled, somehow safe. You protect your own energy and minimize demands. But somewhere there remains a slight feeling of being cut off. Awareness: Is this withdrawal just relaxation – or avoidance? Is there someone you miss without admitting it to yourself? Exercise: Plan a small, concrete contact moment today – short, measured, on your terms. Not because you have to, but because connection also nourishes you.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: You need more information, more time, more analysis – before a decision is made. The inner impulse: If I only know enough, I certainly won't be wrong. But you never know enough. Awareness: At what point would you have enough information - and does this point really exist? What would happen if you decided now, with what you know? Exercise: Set an information limit: Allow yourself one more source, one conversation, one more analysis. Then decide – even if the knowledge still feels incomplete.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: You withdraw – you need distance, silence, time. The other person experiences this as indifference or coldness, which often exacerbates the crisis. A lot is processed inside that is hardly visible from the outside. Awareness: Does the other person need a signal that you are still there - even if you need distance? What would be the smallest sign you could give him? Exercise: Write a short message to the other person, even if you can't talk yet: "I'm still here. I need some time. I'll be back." That keeps the connection.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: Self-doubt takes the form of fear of incompetence: I don't know enough, I don't understand enough, I'm not competent enough for this situation. Retreating into more analysis provides security - but does not solve the doubt. Awareness: What if you were competent enough to handle this situation with what you already know? What would change if you trusted this assessment? Exercise: Decide or act once without further preparation. Name what was good - not what was missing. Build a different inner narrative pattern.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: Loss is processed internally, often without showing it. You think about the loss, analyze it - but the emotional depth remains private, sometimes so private that it cannot unfold. Awareness: What if today you not only understood the loss - but also felt it? Is there someone you could show this to? Exercise: Today, write down what you've lost and what you're feeling in an uncensored, private text. No analysis, no explanation - just feeling in words.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: Overwhelm leads to withdrawal: you need space, time, silence. Social requirements are reduced. This provides short-term relief - but if the withdrawal becomes too long, isolation increases. Awareness: How much withdrawal do you really need – and at what point does it become harmful? Is there anyone you'd like to tell briefly today how you're feeling? Exercise: Write a list today: What can I really leave out? What do i have to do? What can I delegate? Then act according to this list - not according to feeling.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SE5. Autopilot: Stagnation leads to more withdrawal: you read, think, collect - but don't act. Analyzing stagnation replaces breaking through. Withdrawal becomes a comfortable habit. Awareness: What would be the smallest possible step outward – not the perfect one, the smallest one? What if you left him today? Exercise: Today, choose one thing that you have known for a long time but have not done. Do it in twenty minutes. Don't prepare - just start.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: You retreat into your intellect and observe your own stagnation from a clinical distance: analyzing it, categorizing it, and explaining it away. But intellectually understanding the void doesn't dissolve it—it only prolongs it. Awareness: What if you stopped analyzing the standstill today and simply did something—anything small, tangible, and immediate? Exercise: Go outside today and do something physical with your hands: garden, cook, or build something. No abstract thinking allowed. Just act, and feel whatever naturally unfolds in the process.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: In conflict, analysis comes to the fore. You try to understand the situation, recognize patterns, clarify it rationally - while the emotional content of the conflict remains untouched. Awareness: Are you currently analyzing the conflict – or are you really there? What do you feel when you stop analyzing? Exercise: Tell the other person how you feel about this conflict - not what you think. One sentence: “I just feel...”

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: Solitude is filled with knowledge – books, analyses, concepts. You retreat into your intellect and give your loneliness a framework: I am researching, therefore I am there. But the emptiness beneath the thought remains. Awareness: What is your mind looking for right now that knowledge cannot give? Is there a connection you want but don't say? Exercise: Swap a book for a conversation today with someone you feel intellectually connected to. Not to analyze. To really be there.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: You look for the most theoretically coherent system, the model that logically resolves the decision. The analysis is becoming more thorough and comprehensive - but the decision itself is being delayed further and further. Awareness: Beneath all the analysis, is there a hidden sense of what you really want? And would it be possible to follow this hunch – even without the perfect system behind it? Exercise: Write the decision question on a piece of paper. Then, in two minutes, without thinking, write the first answer that comes. Read them. This is often close to the truth.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: You analyze the crisis: What went wrong? What are the underlying patterns? The analysis provides structure - but it does not replace the conversation that would actually be necessary. Awareness: You may understand the crisis better than you experience it. What if you analyzed less and just were there more - with the other person, in this moment? Exercise: Sit down with the other person – without analysis, without explanation. Just: “How are you?” and then: really listen without translating the conversation into a model.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: Self-doubt is directed at the thinking itself: Is my model really correct? Did I miss something? The analysis begins to turn against itself - you doubt your own conclusions. Awareness: Is there a level beyond thought where you know what applies? What does the quiet silence tell you when you stop analyzing? Exercise: Spend twenty minutes today without intellectual activity. Then ask yourself: What do I actually think – not analytically, but simply? Write that down.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: You step back internally: the loss is observed instead of felt. You collect thoughts, read about grief, understand the process - but keep your distance from your own emotional reality. Awareness: What if you didn't think about grief today and just mourned? What would that enable? Exercise: Go for a walk today for half an hour, with no destination and no thought task. Let whatever comes come – including the pain. He can be there.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: You retreat into thinking: analyze the excessive demands, develop systems, read about stress management. This gives a feeling of control - but rarely actually relieves the pressure. Awareness: What if you didn't think about the excessive demands today, but actually did one thing about it or let it go? Exercise: Today, choose the one task that is most pressing. Do them first, without any further planning. Just start. Watch how that feels.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SO5. Autopilot: You retreat into your thinking and observe the stagnation from the outside: analyze, categorize, understand. But understanding emptiness does not eliminate it - it prolongs it. Awareness: What if you stopped analyzing today and just did something – something small, concrete, now? Exercise: Go outside today and do something with your hands: gardening, cooking, doing some crafting. No thinking. Just do and feel what arises.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: Without an all-consuming relationship or a deeply intense project to occupy your mind, your life feels incredibly flat. You sit around waiting for that one special topic or that one electric encounter to make everything feel alive again—missing what is right in front of you. Awareness: What is actually present in your life right now, even if it doesn't feel like the most thrilling thing in the world? Is there a tiny, ordinary step worth taking? Exercise: Connect briefly with someone who matters to you today—keep it short, with no pressure to force a deep conversation. Sometimes, feeling alive begins with a single, simple spark of contact.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: In conflict there is either surprising intensity – a sudden, deep reaction – or complete switching off. Both extremes can confuse the other. Awareness: What is happening inside you right now before you switch off – or before the intensity erupts? Is there a moment in between? Exercise: Stay in the middle: neither switch off nor break out. Say what you perceive: “I notice that I want to withdraw.” Not more.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: Loneliness triggers an intense search for connection - but only the right one, the really real one. Superficial contact feels worse than being alone. The high bar makes connection rare. Awareness: Are you waiting for the perfect connection – and ignoring the people who are actually there? What do you really need from a connection? Exercise: Find contact with someone today without assuming depth. Let the connection be what it is right now - even if it is imperfect.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: You wait for certainty, for the undoubted sign, for the moment when the right option is clear. The waiting time is getting longer. And because no option feels completely safe, you keep postponing. Awareness: How much certainty do you really need to make a decision - and does this certainty even exist? What if you just choose and then trust yourself? Exercise: Decide now – with what you have. Write down the choice and say out loud: I have decided. Watch how that feels.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: You withdraw completely or look for just the right connection – now, intensively. Mediocre contact feels worse than being alone in a crisis. Awareness: Would the person who is there right now – even if they don’t fit perfectly – perhaps be enough to carry this moment together? Exercise: Reach out to someone close to you - not with the expectation of the perfect encounter, but simply: I need connection right now.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: The self-doubt is about connection: Am I really capable of maintaining this deep connection that I desire? Am I too intense, too strange, too demanding? Withdrawal protects against the answer. Awareness: What if you're just the right person for a deep connection - and you're not showing enough of it? Exercise: Show something real about yourself to the person you are close to today - without filtering it first. A real thought, a real feeling. Watch what happens then.

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: Loss in deep relationships hits particularly hard - and is particularly protected. You withdraw, process things alone, don't let anyone close. Withdrawal protects but prolongs isolation. Awareness: Is there someone you could tell today what you've lost - without having to explain everything? Just show. Exercise: Reach out to someone you trust today - not to talk, but to not be alone. Just say, "I'm grieving right now. Can you be near?"

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: Overwhelm occurs when the outside world and relationship demands become too much. You retreat into intensive worlds of thought or individual projects - and lose contact with the reality of the requirements. Awareness: What is the one specific thing you need to do today - beyond all thought? Can you prioritize that? Exercise: Set a specific time limit for yourself today: two hours for the most important task. Then an hour for you. Keep both.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SX5. Autopilot: Without an intense connection or deep project, everything feels flat. You wait for that one topic, that one encounter that will bring everything back to life - and miss what is there now. Awareness: What’s there right now – even if it’s not the most intense thing? Is there something small that would be worth a step? Exercise: Get in touch with someone who is important to you today – just briefly, without any pretense of depth. Sometimes life begins with a small contact.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Stagnation triggers intense anxiety: What if things stay like this forever? What if I'm falling behind everyone else? Worrying about the future makes the present standstill feel unbearable. You try to find safety by building elaborate plans instead of grounding yourself in the now. Awareness: What if you are neither moving forward nor falling behind right now—but simply conserving your energy and gathering strength? Could this standstill actually be a necessary rest? Exercise: Today, write down a list of what is currently stable and reliable in your life. Don't focus on what is missing—focus on what is holding you up. Read that list to yourself three times.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Fear can arise in conflict – fear of losing the relationship, of chaos, of doing the wrong thing. This shows itself either as a search for protection or as a hardening: I am right and will defend it. Awareness: What do you really fear behind this conflict? And is this fear really what is happening? Exercise: Separate the actual issue of conflict from the fear underneath. Quietly name the fear – and only then: What is the actual issue?

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Loneliness activates fear: is this normal? Did I do something wrong? Will I be excluded? The mind begins to analyze and insure instead of simply seeking connection. Awareness: What if loneliness is simply a pause – not a sign of danger, not a sign of mistake? Exercise: Reach out to someone you trust - not with a question, but with an invitation: Let's spend time together. Trust the impulse without analyzing it first.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Decisions trigger catastrophic thinking: What if this is wrong? What are the worst consequences? The mind develops scenarios that make the decision seem increasingly risky. Awareness: How likely is the worst case scenario really - and have you ever made a decision and survived that felt like that at the time? Exercise: Write down the worst case scenario. Then write what you would do in this case. When you know this, fear has less power over the decision.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Fear dominates: Will I lose this relationship? Am I to blame? What do others think about it? You seek security through questions, security, analysis - and this often makes the crisis bigger. Awareness: What do you really know right now - and what are you afraid of? And is there anyone you trust who could help you separate this? Exercise: Speak to the other person calmly and directly: "I'm worried about us. How do you see that?" Then hear the answer without immediately judging or catastrophizing it.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Self-doubt is fueled by fear: Am I really sure I'm doing this right? What if I'm wrong? What if others see through this? The inner criticism charges every uncertainty with a threat. Awareness: What if you were allowed to be insecure - and that still wasn't a sign that there was something fundamentally wrong with you? Exercise: When self-doubt arises, name it out loud: "This is fear, not truth." Then ask yourself: What would a calm, well-meaning observer say?

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Loss triggers fear: what comes next? How safe am I? The pain is mixed with worry about the future. You look for security, advice, confirmation - instead of facing the grief directly. Awareness: What if you put aside worry about the future today – just for an hour – and just mourn what is now? Exercise: Write down: What have I lost and what is still there? Not to minimize the pain - to see the foundation that supports.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Overwhelm activates fear: What if I can't do it? What if something goes wrong? You look for protection, ask others, plan twice. The pressure increases with the worry. Awareness: What's the worst that can really happen - and how likely is that? Realistically, what would be enough? Exercise: Write down today: What do I really need to do, and what am I just afraid I need to do? Separate both. Only act on the first list.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SE6. Autopilot: Stagnation triggers fear: What if it stays that way forever? What if I lose connection? Concern about the future makes standing still more difficult. You look for security in plans instead of in the now. Awareness: What if you were neither moving forward nor falling behind - but gathering strength? Could this also be the standstill? Exercise: Write down today: What is stable in my life right now? Not what is missing - what contributes. Read the list three times.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: Without a clear group task or a sense of belonging to a system, you face a sudden loss of direction: *What is my role? Where do I fit in?* You frantically search for external structure and alignment instead of looking for internal direction. Awareness: What if you are important right now not because of a group or a structure—but simply for your own sake? What value do you carry within yourself? Exercise: Do something today that belongs entirely to you—not a project for the group, and not a contribution for others. Just for you. Observe how that feels.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: In the conflict, reference is made to what is usual, what the group expects, what the rules say. Your own position is formulated less as a personal opinion and more as what you do. Awareness: What is your own opinion in this conflict - regardless of what others expect or what the norm says? Exercise: Formulate your point of view in a very personal way: “I personally want to…” Observe how that feels.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: Loneliness within the group feels paradoxical: you are surrounded by people, but still alone. The feeling of belonging is missing, even though you belong. The search for the right system, the right community continues. Awareness: Do you seek belonging through meeting expectations – or through truly showing who you are? Do the people in your group know what really concerns you? Exercise: Today, tell someone in your group something really personal—not an opinion about the group, but something about yourself. Watch how this changes the connection.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: You seek security through group decision: What would the community choose? What is the consensus? Your own position disappears behind what the system approves. Awareness: What would you choose if you didn't need the group's approval? Is there an opinion in you that you haven't spoken out loud yet? Exercise: Share your own position – even if it differs from the group consensus. Say it as a personal opinion, not as truth. Observe what this triggers in you.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: You ask the group: What would others do in my position? What is normal, what is acceptable? Your own assessment of the crisis takes a back seat in favor of the collective judgment. Awareness: What do you know – within yourself, calmly, independently of others – about this relationship situation? This voice has the most right. Exercise: Write down how you assess the crisis - without seeking advice, without comparison. Only you, your perception, your assessment. Then decide how you want to act.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: You doubt whether you are living up to the system, the group, the expectations. Am I really loyal enough? Am I doing the right thing? Self-doubt is tied to the collective judgment: What would the group think? Awareness: Whose opinion are you currently asking internally - and do you also trust yourself? What would you rate if you couldn't ask anyone? Exercise: Cases today require a small assessment or decision without consultation. Then observe: Did the world depend on it? And: Was your assessment so wrong?

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: You look for support in the community: rituals, groups, traditions help. But sometimes one's own pain remains hidden under the collective framework because it is easier to bear than to feel. Awareness: Is there something in this loss that is only yours - and that you haven't really felt yet? Exercise: Take half an hour alone today - no group, no community. Just you and your loss. Then come back and say a sentence about it to someone.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: You take responsibility for the system, the group, the expectations of others - and forget your own boundaries. Loyal and reliable until exhaustion. Awareness: What are you taking on that isn't your job? And what would be the first step to giving that back? Exercise: Talk to someone in the team or group today: “I need help with…” Be specific about what you need. Let others participate.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SO6. Autopilot: Without a group task or system affiliation, there is a risk of loss of orientation: What is my role? What do I belong to? You look for structure and connection instead of inner direction. Awareness: What if you are important not because of a group or structure - but for yourself? What do you carry within you? Exercise: Do something today that is just yours - not a project for the group, not a contribution to others. Only for you. Watch how that feels.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Stagnation triggers a tense cycle of paralysis and rebellion: you either aggressively fight against the standstill and run blindly forward, or you freeze up completely. You rarely allow yourself to just tolerate the internal emptiness. Awareness: What if you chose neither to fight nor to freeze today—but simply sat still and watched whatever comes up? Exercise: Pause right in the middle of the emptiness today. Spend ten minutes completely free of distractions. Then ask yourself: *What is quietly calling out from the depths?* Write it down.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: In conflict, the energy can spill outward - confrontational, direct, challenging. Sometimes you test whether the other person can really hold up. This can escalate. Awareness: Are you currently testing the other one – and what do you hope will happen? Do you trust the outcome, no matter what it turns out to be? Exercise: Before you confront: ask instead of demanding. “I don’t understand right now – what do you mean?” See if this opens up the space.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Loneliness creates mistrust: Why aren't the others there? What's behind it? You scan the situation for danger and at the same time withdraw yourself - which increases the loneliness. Awareness: Do you distrust being alone right now - or do you distrust people who aren't there? What would happen if you trusted the impulse to connect? Exercise: Test your trust today: Reach out to someone without knowing how they will react. Leave open what comes.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Decisions are either made boldly and confrontationally – against the grain, against expectations – or endlessly postponed as the danger of each option is analyzed. Both can be paralyzing. Awareness: Are you making decisions based on strength – or against fear? And would the decision be the same if the fear wasn't there? Exercise: Ask yourself: What would I choose if I had neither fear of doing wrong nor the impulse to appear bold? This neutral answer is often the correct one.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Either the crisis escalates - you fight, confront, blame the other person for everything - or you flee: new activities, other contacts, everything except the actual conversation. Awareness: Does fighting or fleeing protect you – or does it deepen the crisis? What if you just stood still for a moment? Exercise: Calmly tell the other person what hurt you - without blame, without drama. Just: "That hit me because..." Nothing more. Watch what happens then.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Self-doubt easily turns into distrust: Is what I think really true? And if it's true, am I brave enough to do it? Or too cowardly? You doubt your assessment and your own reaction to it. Awareness: What do you know right now – not what you fear? And what would a brave but calm person in your situation do now? Exercise: Make a small, clear decision today without long consideration. Then stand by it, even if doubts arise. Watch: What's Really Happening?

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Loss creates inner conflict: the pain is there, but you doubt it. Was it really that important? Could I have prevented it? The grief oscillates between intensity and self-doubt. Awareness: What if your pain is justified – without justification, without comparison? He's just there. That's enough. Exercise: Write a sentence today: "I mourn... because..." Leave it there without questioning it. That's enough.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Excessive demands create conflict: on the one hand you fight against it (counterphobic), on the other hand fear paralyzes action. You alternate between being overwhelmed and being frozen. Awareness: What would be the next small, safe step – not the whole solution, just the next step? Exercise: Write down the three most urgent tasks. Then do the first one – only the first one. Everything else doesn't exist for now. Watch what solves this.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SX6. Autopilot: Stagnation oscillates between paralysis and rebellion: either you fight it and run, or you freeze. The inner emptiness is rarely simply endured. Awareness: What if you didn't fight or paralyze today - but just sit and see what comes? Exercise: Pause in the midst of emptiness today. Ten minutes without distractions. Then ask: What speaks quietly from the depths? Write it down.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: Stagnation feels utterly intolerable to your system: you instantly jump to the next concept, the next thrill, or the next elaborate plan. You aggressively fill the internal void before it has a single chance to say anything meaningful to you. Awareness: What if you deliberately chose not to fill the emptiness today—and instead waited to see what it wants to show you? What have you been tuning out up until now? Exercise: Sit for half an hour today with no plan, no goal, and no distractions. When the internal restlessness inevitably hits, don't move. Just stay. Observe what is resting right beneath the noise.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: In conflict, the reframing impulse comes into force: the glass half full is emphasized, the problem is downplayed, the topic is redirected. You want to resolve the conflict – without really getting into it. Awareness: What is being buried beneath the humor or redirection right now – and what if you let it stay on top? Exercise: Stay with an unpleasant moment of conflict without lightening it or redirecting it. Keep the space open. Watch what comes next.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: Loneliness is diverted away – new plans, new ideas, new distractions. You convince yourself that you like being alone, that you need freedom. Sometimes there is a longing underneath that you don't want to admit to yourself. Awareness: What if you didn't try to eliminate loneliness, but actually sat in it for a moment? What comes next? Exercise: Sit for ten minutes today with no plan, no next idea. Let the silence come. What happens when the noise stops?

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: You jump to the decision quickly – to keep your options open, to avoid the discomfort of waiting. At the same time, the alternatives are kept in mind. You've decided, but you haven't really let go yet. Awareness: Have you really made this decision – or are you still keeping it open? What if you actually complete it now? Exercise: Make a decision – and consciously close the door to the alternatives. Say out loud: I'm letting go of this option. Observe what this triggers in you.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: People reframe the crisis: “This is just a difficult phase,” “We are currently growing,” “It will get better.” The actual tension is reinterpreted instead of looked at. The other person doesn't feel heard. Awareness: What if you left the crisis as it is - without trying to make it any better? What would you see and say then? Exercise: Tell the other person: "I notice that things are not going well between us right now." Without a solution, without a positive framework. Just perception, clear and direct.

Situation "Self-doubt & inner criticism" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: Self-doubt is quickly eliminated: This will get better, I can do it, no need to worry. But underneath sometimes lies a deeper question that is never asked: Am I really enough - when the shine is gone? Awareness: What if you really let self-doubt sit - just for a moment, without solving it? What is he showing you? Exercise: Write down what you doubt about yourself - honestly, without making light of it. Then ask yourself: What about this doubt is real evidence, and what is fear in disguise?

Situation "Loss & grief" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: Loss is quickly reframed: It's getting better, I'm learning from it, maybe that was a good thing. The reframing strategy protects from the full pain - and sometimes from what he wants to say. Awareness: What if you didn’t reframe that loss today – but just lost it? What would that show? Exercise: Today, sit with what you have lost for ten minutes - without reinterpreting it, without enriching it. Only: That's gone. That hurts. Let that be true.

Situation "Overwhelm & pressure" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: Excessive demands are explained away or redirected: There are still so many exciting possibilities, new ideas, other projects. The pressure is reduced by distraction instead of released. Awareness: What if you stick with what's currently pressing today - without moving on to the next idea? What then appears? Exercise: Today, choose the one task that has been waiting the longest. Set a timer for 45 minutes. Just this task. No switching, no distractions. Then see what you've accomplished.

Situation "Stagnation & inner emptiness" for subtype SE7. Autopilot: Stagnation is perceived as unbearable: you jump to the next idea, the next experience, the next plan. The void is immediately filled before she can say anything. Awareness: What if you don't fill the void today - and wait to see what it shows? What have you perhaps missed so far? Exercise: Sit today for half an hour with no plan, no goal, no distraction. When trouble comes, stay. Observe what lies beneath.

Situation "Exhaustion & burnout" for subtype SO7. Autopilot: You bridge the internal emptiness with grand visions and future plans: the next big project, the next adventure, the next source of meaning. The actual stagnation remains invisible behind your wall of ideas. Awareness: What if you chose not to map out a brand-new vision today—and instead just sat with the present moment? What is actually here right now? Exercise: Spend an entire evening tonight without making any plans. No notebooks, no brainstorming. Just ask: *What is right now?* Let the answer emerge in total stillness.

Situation "Conflict & dispute" for subtype SO7. Autopilot: In conflicts, reconciliation and the good ending are quickly brought into focus - sometimes before the actual pain was really there. You want to go back into the bright room. Awareness: Would this conflict be allowed to continue for a while - and that that be okay? Exercise: Stay in the discomfort of the conflict for a while without pushing for resolution. Ask the other person, “What do you need right now?” Really listen.

Situation "Loneliness & withdrawal" for subtype SO7. Autopilot: Loneliness takes on a greater meaning: you dedicate yourself to the community, to a project, to an idea. Your own loneliness disappears in the service of something greater. But underneath there remains a longing for real personal connection. Awareness: Who are you close to right now – really close, as a person, not as a comrade-in-arms? Is there someone who knows you, not just appreciates you? Exercise: Looking for a personal encounter today – without project reference, without a group setting. Just two people together. Observe what this moves within you.

Situation "Decision making stress" for subtype SO7. Autopilot: You frame the decision so that every option sounds positive - an internal reframing that makes the choice seem easier. But underneath there remains the unresolved question of which option is really the right one. Awareness: What if you looked at the decision without a positive frame? What would you see then – and what would you choose? Exercise: Write down what is really difficult about each option. Then choose anyway. Not because it's easy - but because it gets you further.

Situation "Relationship crisis" for subtype SO7. Autopilot: You dedicate yourself to the community, an idea, a project - and the personal relationship crisis takes on a greater scope. What really needs to be said between two people remains unsaid. Awareness: Are you currently hiding behind a larger task - so you don't have to face the silence of this one relationship? Exercise: Spend time with this person today – just the two of you, with no task, no project. Let what needs to arise arise.
